background.definition: Alcohol withdrawal refers to a spectrum of signs and symptoms that can range from irritability and tremors to hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens when a heavy drinker suddenly decreases or ceases consumption.

list.listitem: In 2004, 365,000 patients were discharged with a diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal, delirium, or psychosis.
The incidence of alcohol withdrawal is about 5% in placebo-treated patients entered into clinical trials involving inpatients with alcohol related concerns.
Withdrawal symptoms occur in 15% to 20% of primary care and hospitalized patients.
Sudden decrease or cessation of consumption of alcohol in a heavy drinker.
Alcohol acts at the level of the central nervous system to inhibit excitatory neurotransmitters and to enhance inhibitory neurons, leading to an overall depression of the central nervous system.
When alcohol is removed, the reverse takes place and excitatory processes are enhanced and inhibitory processes are diminished. The GABA system is most directly affected.
Norepinephrine, and serotonin neurotransmitter systems have also been implicated.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of previous episodes of withdrawal
Use of medications known to lower the seizure threshold
Presence of comorbid disease state (risk for delirium tremons)
Greater number of days since last drink (risk for delirium tremens)

list.listitem: The USPTF recommends screening and behavioral interventions to reduce alcohol misuse by adults, including pregnant women, in primary care. A

The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline recommends universal screening for unhealthy alcohol use including assessing for risk of developing alcohol withdrawal in persons known to be using alcohol recently, regularly, and heavily.
Formal questionnaires (CAGE score, AUDIT-C) can help detect alcohol overuse. A
Society of Academic Emergency Medicine recommend naltrexone, acamprosate or gabapentin to prevent a return to heavy drinking for patients with AWS. A
The CIWA-Ar is a reproducible and valid withdrawal-severity assessment scale. A
Blood alcohol content should be measured in a seizure of unknown etiology or if alcohol withdrawal is suspected but not confirmed by history. C
Neuorimaging is indicated for an initial seizure or if a seizure pattern changes. An EEG should be performed after a first seizure of after subsequent seizures if the diagnosis is in question. B

Differential.Differential_Features: History of alcohol use disorders . After primary seizure, patients are typically calm. In alcohol-withdrawal seizure, patient remains agitated
History of alcohol use disorder ; positive screening result
History of alcohol use disorder , positive screening, absence of symptoms with withdrawal medications

list.listitem: Clinically, patients with mild or uncomplicated withdrawal present with restlessness, irritability, anorexia, anxiety, and insomnia.
Patients with complicated or severe withdrawal may have delirium, hallucinations, delusions, seizures, or changes in body temperature, pulse, or blood pressure.

A history of alcohol consumption should be obtained with supplementary information supplied by family and/or friends. The quantity and frequency of consumption as well as any change in the pattern of use should be documented. The time of last alcohol consumption should be established. A history of previous alcohol-withdrawal syndromes (seizure, delerium tremens, etc.) should be recorded.
Polysubstance use should be screened for and assessed.
Conduct a neurological exam in patients presenting with a seizure and/or delirium.

When information about recent alcohol use is unavailable or unreliable, biomarkers for alcohol use can be used. These include carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) and gammaglutamyl transferase (GGT). These tests have poor accuracy when applied to the general public.
Blood alcohol concentrations should be measured in persons suspected of having an alcohol-related seizure.

Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) is indicated for the initial seizure of if there is a change in seizure type or frequency or if the seizure is otherwise atypical (greater than 48 hours after cessation of drinking).
EEG should be performed after the first seizure and after repeated seizures if a secondary or alternative etiology is suspected.
Identify concurrent conditions: medical conditions that could affect the course of alcohol withdrawal, pregnancy test as appropriate, CBC, metabolic profile and lever tests.
Nutritional deficiencies should be assessed and treated as appropriate.
The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment Scale (CIWA-ar) can be used to predict the severity of alcohol withdrawal. It is also available as an interactive calculator.
Formal questionnaires (e.g., CAGE score, AUDIT-C) can help to detect alcohol overuse.
Alcohol withdrawal and alcohol withdrawal delirium should be diagnosed using DSM-5.

A clinical prediction rule identified 8 independent risk factors for severe alcohol withdrawal including seizure history, elevated bilirubin, elevated AST, depression, tachycardia, white race, low potassium, and presenting for a diagnosis other than alcohol use disorder. The presence of 3 or more of the 8 risk factors predicted severe disease.

The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment-Alcohol (CIWA-A) and the shortened CIWA-A, revised (CIWA-Ar), are reproducible and valid withdrawal-severity assessment scales. It does not diagnose withdrawal. See the interactive clinical decision rule.

A score of <8 to 10 is considered mild withdrawal, a score of 8 to 15 is considered moderate withdrawal, and a score >15 is considered severe withdrawal. Patients with delirium, hallucinations, seizure, body temperature changes, tachycardia, and hypertension should also be considered to have severe withdrawal.
See for dosing recommendations.

Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal. They should be administered prophylactically to all patients with severe withdrawal symptoms and in patients with a history of previous withdrawal seizure. A
The CIWA-aR can be used to guide decisions regarding administration of medication. A
Symptom-triggered administration of benzodiazepine is safe and leads to smaller quantities of medication needed to control symptoms. B
Definitive conclusions regarding the safety and efficacy of anticonvulsants cannot be reached currently. B
Adjunctive agents such as beta-blockers and clonidine reduce the signs and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal but should not be used as the sole agent in withdrawal. A

Society for Academic Emergnecy Medicine guidelines for management of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) recommend benzodiapines + phenobarbital for adults with moderate to severe AWS who are being admitted.
Thiamine 100 mg IV or IM daily for at least 3 days is recommended for patients with alcohol-withdrawal delirium.
Thiamine should be given prior to administering glucose if needed.

Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal. They should be administered prophylactically to all patients with severe withdrawal symptoms or in patients with a history of previous alcohol-withdrawal seizures. They are superior to placebo in reducing signs and symptoms of withdrawal, especially seizure (risk reduction of 7.7 seizures per 100 patients treated). It is difficult to assess the relative effectiveness and safety of benzodiazepines compared with other drugs because of the heterogeneity in interventions and assessment of outcomes.

The initial therapeutic goal of alcohol withdrawal is rapid control of agitation. When treating alcohol-withdrawal delirium, benzodiazepines with rapid onset of action control agitation more quickly, but longer acting agents provide a smoother treatment course and have fewer breakthrough symptoms. Shorter acting agents may be preferred if there is a concern about sedation or in patients with comorbid disease or liver disease.

Symptom-triggered medication administration led to a decrease in the amount of benzodiazepine needed to control withdrawal symptoms compared with a fixed-dose administration scheme. There was no difference in patient comfort or complications (seizure or delirium). Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine administration also led to less total medication needed compared with fixed-dosing schedules. Both schemes were effective in preventing complications of alcohol withdrawal.

A retrospective cohort study found that symptom triggered dosing was associated with lower amount and duration of benzodiazepine use in a population of adults 70 years and older admitted for alcohol withdrawal syndrome.

All benzodiazepines appear to be similarly effective in reducing signs and symptoms of withdrawal. Longer acting agents may be more effective in preventing seizures but may lead to excess sedation. Shorter acting agents may be useful when rapid control of symptoms is necessary but have more potential for misuse. See for dosing recommendations.

The dose of sedative-hypnotic medication for treatment should be individualized to the patient. The therapeutic goal is light somnolence. Doses of sedative-hypnotic used to control alcohol-withdrawal delirium may be much higher than doses needed to treat anxiety or presurgical sedation. Occasionally, massive doses of benzodiazepine may be needed to control symptoms. Patients may require care in an intensive care unit.

The initial treatment of alcohol-related status epilepticus is IV lorazepam. Lorazepam 2 mg IV has also been shown to reduce the risk of a second seizure in persons with chronic alcohol use presenting to the emergency department with a witnessed generalized seizure (3% vs. 24%; NNT 4.8).

The safety and effectiveness of anticonvulsants in alcohol withdrawal are inconclusive. Phenytoin (15 mg/kg IV) given after the first witnessed seizure failed to prevent a second seizure in a 6-hour observation period. Carbamazepine is superior to placebo and equal in efficacy to oxazepam in treating mild to moderate withdrawal symptoms. Its efficacy in treating or preventing withdrawal seizures and delirium is unknown.

A single dose of IV phenobarbitol (10 mg/kg) plus use of a symptom-guided lorazepam-based withdrawal protocol was associated with fewer ICU admissions (8% vs. 25% for placebo) in 102 patients presenting to the ED with AWS, and was not associated with increased adverse outcomes.

A systematic review identified 2 RCTs and 6 observational studies, and concluded that treatment with phenobarbital does not reduce ICU admissions, hospital admissions, readmissions or adverse events compared with benzodiazepines. Two additional systematic reviews of came to a similar conclusion.

Beta-blockers reduce the signs and symptoms of withdrawal, but the effects on seizure activity are unknown. Beta-blockers may increase delirium and may mask development of significant withdrawal symptoms. They are not recommended for routine use in alcohol-withdrawal delirium but may be used in combination with benzodiazepines in selected patients with hypertension and/or tachycardia.
Clonidine has been shown to be effective for reducing symptoms in patients with mild to moderate withdrawal. Its effects on seizure and delirium are unknown.

Dexmedetomidine is from the same drug class as clonidine (centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic agonists) and was studied in a small RCT of 24 patients with a CIWA score ≥15 despite receiving at least 16 mg lorazepam over 4 hours. Those randomized to addition of dexmedetomidine (0.4-1.2 mcg/kg/h) required less lorazepam in the next 24 hours (56 mg vs. 8 mg) but long-term lorazepam requirements and other outcomes were similar between groups. A systematic review of RCTs and cohort studies concluded that there was no significant benefit to adding dexmedetomidine.

Neuroleptic agents are less effective than benzodiazepines in treating signs and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal and may lower seizure threshold, but they may be useful to calm agitated patients. They should not be used as the sole treatment agent in alcohol-withdrawal delirium. If extremely large doses of benzodiazepines fail to control agitation, pentobarbitol or propofol may be used. However, the latter is frequently associated with hypotension and the need for mechanical ventilation.

Baclofen (30/mg daily for 10 days) was as effective as diazepam (0.5-0.75 mg/kg for 6 consecutive days, followed by a tapering dose of 25%/day on days 7-10) in reducing symptoms of uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal. However a Cochrane review (which included this study) concluded that the evidence for recommending baclofen for the AWS is insufficient and of too low quality to draw any firm conclusions.

Magnesium supplementation does not reduce signs and symptoms of withdrawal, and a Cochrane review concluded that there was insufficient evidence to determine if it is beneficial or harmful in the treatment or prevention of AWS. Ethyl alcohol is not recommend for treatment of alcohol-withdrawal delirium.

In a small RCT, intranasal oxytocin (24 IU/dose twice daily for 3 days) was found to decrease withdrawal symptoms in patients with alcohol tolerance, and was associated with less benzodiazepam use and lower CIWA withdrawal scores.
The opioid receptor blocker nalmefene has been studied in 5 RCTs with 2567 patients had minimal benefits, decreasing heavy drinking days by only 1.6 per month.
A pilot study failed to show benefit of auricular laser acupuncture in reducing alcohol-withdrawal symptoms.
Massage decreases scores on the Alcohol Withdrawal Scale early in treatment and decreases pulse rate in later days of treatment when used as a complementary therapy.
After detoxification, the patient's underlying alcohol use disorder should be treated, with relapse prevention being stressed.
Expert opinion holds that, in patients with alcohol-withdrawal delirium, a quiet room with good lighting and appropriate environmental clues may reduce confusion.
Decisions to determine level of care can be aided by American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Placement Criteria.

Assessment of immediate needs includes acute intoxication and/or withdrawal potential, biomedical conditions and complications, emotional/behavioral/cognitive conditions, readiness to change, relapse/continued use/continued problem potential, recovery environment.

Hospitalization is indicated in patients who have an overdose or cannot be safely monitored in an outpatient or emergency department setting, have risk factors for having severe or complicated withdrawal symptoms, have medical or psychiatric comorbidities that make outpatient detoxification unsafe, have behavioral health concerns that make the patient a danger to self or others, or have not responded to less intensive levels of care.
Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale (PAWSS) can be used for hospitalized patients to predict risk of developing severe or complicated alcohol withdrawal.
For patients who do not meet criteria; for inpatient withdrawal treatment the ASAM Placement Criteria may help establish an appropriate level of care.
Patients should be monitored for signs of hypoglycemia.

The initial treatment of alcohol-related status epilepticus is IV lorazepam. Lorazepam 2 mg IV has also been shown to reduce the risk of a second seizure in persons with an alcohol use disorder presenting to the emergency department with a witnessed generalized seizure (3% vs. 24%; NNT 4.8).
If electrolyte abnormalities are discovered, they should be corrected.
Respiratory depression may require intubation.

Significant medical comorbidities, a history of complicated withdrawal, gastrointestinal pathology, renal or hepatic insufficiency, prolonged hyperthermia, or a need for frequent or high-dose sedatives require hospitalization and, if significant, ICU admission.
Alcohol-withdrawal symptoms typically start within 4 to 12 hours after cessation of alcohol, peak within 24 to 48 hours, and resolve within 4 to 5 days. B

Minor withdrawal symptoms (insomnia, tremulousness, headache, diaphoresis, anorexia) can occur within 6 hours of cessation and while the blood alcohol level is still positive; withdrawal seizures typically occur within 48 hours of cessation, and hallucinations develop after about 12 to 24 hours after cessation and resolve within 24 to 48 hours. Alcohol withdrawal can occur from a decrease in alcohol consumption and not complete cessation. C

Alcohol-withdrawal delirium complicates about 5% of alcohol-withdrawal syndromes. Mortality rates for alcohol withdrawal were once reported at 15%, but, with the advent of benzodiazepine treatment and improved supportive care, those rates have fallen to between 0 and 1%. A

Alcohol-withdrawal management should be considered the first step in treatment. All persons who receive treatment for alcohol withdrawal should be offered treatment for their alcohol use disorder as soon as cognitive status permits.

A clinical prediction rule identified 8 independent risk factors for severe alcohol withdrawal including seizure history, elevated bilirubin, elevated AST, depression, tachycardia, white race, low potassium, and presenting for a diagnosis other than alcohol use disorder. The presence of 3 or more of the 8 risk factors predicted severel disease.
Shorter acting benzodiazepines should be considered in the elderly if there is concern for oversedation.
Benzodiazepines and barbiturates have been associated with adverse fetal outcomes. Medication should be limited to the amount needed to prevent major complications of withdrawal.
Pregnant people should be encouraged to seek further treatment after acute withdrawal and offered support to enter and maintain treatment.
There is no evidence that recommendations should be altered in the adolescent population.

feature.caption: Different Regimens of Benzodiazepine Administration for Alcohol Withdrawal.
feature.feature_body:
Method Description Example When to Consider Drawbacks
Loading dose Administration of a slowly metabolized benzodiazepine every 1-3 h until sedation occurs or until clinical improvement of symptoms is established Diazepam 20 mg or chlordiazepoxide 100 mg or equivalent every 2-3 h Patients at risk for severe complications who are already experiencing withdrawal symptoms Requires hospitalization and intensive monitoring of hemodynamic and respiratory parameters; oversedation is a risk
Symptom triggered With a withdrawal assessment scale, a dose of benzodiazepine is administered according to the score; the process is repeated every 30-60 min depending of the onset of action of the medication until symptoms are controlled For a CIWA-Ar score of <9, no medication is given; for a CIWA-Ar score of 10-15, oxazepam 15 mg or chlordiazepoxide 50 mg or equivalent is given; for a CIWA-Ar score of >15, oxazepam 30 mg or chlordiazepoxide or equivalent is given Patients with no history of complicated withdrawal Requires staff comfortable administering assessment scale and following treatment protocol
Fixed dose with gradual taper The patient is stabilized on a benzodiazepine dose that dose is slowly tapered over 3-5 days depending on patient response to medication Patient is started on oxazepam 30 mg or chlordiazepoxide 100 mg or equivalent for four doses, then given oxazepam 15 mg or chlordiazepoxide 50 mg every 6 h for 8 doses, with additional medication given as needed for breakthrough symptoms Commonly used regimen; adaptable to individual patient Protocols vary widely across institutions; patient must be stabilized prior to taper
Data from Physical detoxification services for withdrawal from specific substances. Center for Substance Abuse Treatment (CSAT). Detoxification and substance abuse treatment. Rockville, MD: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA); 2006 Jan 18. pp. 41-111.
